t: Confusing Number II — Counting Confusing Numbers up to 10^9
o: A number is **confusing** if every digit is one of {0,1,6,8,9} and rotating the whole number 180° yields a *different* value (leading zeros of the rotation are dropped). We must count such numbers in [1, n] where n can be 10^9. Checking each integer from 1 to n is far too slow (10^9 numbers), so we need to generate only candidates built from valid digits — there are at most 5^10 ≈ 9.7M such strings, and pruning by length/value cuts this drastically. For example, for n = 20 we enumerate valid-digit numbers ≤ 20: 1, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 16, 18, 19; rotating each (1→1 invalid, 6→9 ✓, 8→8 invalid, 9→6 ✓, 10→01=1 ✓, 11→11 invalid, 16→91 ✓, 18→81 ✓, 19→61 ✓) gives 6 confusing numbers.
k: Only digits {0,1,6,8,9} may appear, so candidates can be generated directly instead of testing all integers.
A candidate is confusing iff its rotated value differs from itself; compare numerically to handle dropped leading zeros.
Backtracking over digit positions with a bound against n keeps the search tiny (~hundreds of thousands of nodes at most).

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Integers
a.i: Check every number from 1 to n: skip it if any digit is invalid, otherwise build its rotation digit-by-digit (reversed order, mapping 6↔9) and compare with the original. Simple but too slow for n near 10^9 in practice; included as the intuitive baseline.
s: For each x in [1, n], scan its digits; if any digit is not in {0,1,6,8,9}, continue.
Build rot = reverse of x's digits with 6→9, 9→6, others fixed.
If rot != x, increment the answer.
a.t: O(n · d) where d ≈ 10 is the digit count — iterates all n integers and processes their digits.
a.sp: O(d) — temporary strings for one number at a time.

a.n: Approach 2: Backtracking Generation of Valid-Digit Numbers (Optimal)
a.i: Instead of filtering all integers, recursively build numbers using only digits {0,1,6,8,9} while staying ≤ n. At each complete candidate, compute its rotation arithmetically (process digits from least significant, mapping 6↔9) and count it if the rotation differs. The recursion tree has at most 5^10 leaves but pruning by the bound on n keeps it small enough to run instantly.
s: Start a DFS with current value cur = 0; try appending each digit d in {1,6,8,9} first (skip leading zero), then also 0 for deeper levels.
If cur*10 + d > n, prune this branch (digits are tried in increasing order per position, so larger d also fails).
Recurse with next = cur*10 + d; after recursing, evaluate next as a candidate.
To rotate next: repeatedly take next % 10, map via {0:0,1:1,6:9,8:8,9:6}, and accumulate into rev = rev*10 + mapped digit.
Count next if rev != next; return total count.
a.t: O(5^L) where L ≈ log10(n) ≤ 10 is the number of digits — we only visit numbers composed of valid digits and bounded by n (roughly hundreds of thousands of calls worst case), each doing O(L) work for rotation.
a.sp: O(L) — recursion depth equals the maximum number of digits.

w: In an interview, mention the brute-force idea briefly, then pivot to backtracking generation since n up to 10^9 makes per-integer checking infeasible. Pitfalls: forgetting that leading zeros in the rotation are dropped (numeric comparison handles this automatically); counting non-confusing strobogrammatic numbers like 1, 8, 11, 69, 88, 96, 101; overflow when building rotations in fixed-width languages (use 64-bit / Python ints); accidentally allowing a leading 0 in generated candidates. Edge cases: n = 1 → 0, n = 6 → 1, n = 10^9 boundary. Follow-ups: count confusing numbers in a range [l, r] (compute f(r) − f(l−1)), or find the k-th smallest confusing number (order the DFS traversal).
